story.headline: The dollar held most of last Friday's jobs-report jump as Asian stocks bounced and gold rose. Tuesday's US inflation figures now decide whether a December Federal Reserve rate hike, priced near 79%, holds.

reads.policy: A December Federal Reserve hike stays the market's main expectation after last week's strong US jobs report, which keeps rate support under the dollar. Hikes are also expected in Europe and Japan, while job losses in Canada and New Zealand give those banks reasons to wait. Tuesday's US inflation figures are the next big check.
reads.growth: The US job market looks much firmer than Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the US dollar. China's figures showed weak shopping at home, a soft spot for the currencies that sell to it, like the Aussie and the kiwi. UK growth figures on Thursday are the next big read.
reads.inflation: Factory prices in China are climbing fast on dear oil while shop prices cool, so the energy shock is still working through supply chains. US inflation is well above the Fed's goal, and Tuesday's figures will show whether it is cooling. Hot prices would favour the dollar; soft ones would weigh on it.
reads.risk: Asian stocks bounced hard after last week's AI and chip-stock rout, so fear eased and demand for safe havens faded a little. The Aussie and the kiwi, which were hit hardest, won back some ground. News that Nvidia's board is investigating its chief executive barely dented the mood.
reads.tot: Oil held near $98 a barrel as softer US war talk and fresh attacks around the Gulf cancelled each other out. Prices well below October's highs ease the bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. They also give less support to the Canadian dollar.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and over the past month they sharply added to their bets against the kiwi and the euro. In the Aussie and the pound, hedge funds and real-money investors sit on opposite sides, with real money betting heavily against both.
reads.fiscal: No new budget news moved currencies overnight. New Zealand's election count points to the same coalition staying, which lowers the risk of a big budget change. A Democratic Congress still makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. A strong October jobs report has made a December hike the market's main expectation, which supports the dollar.
fed.why: US inflation is well above the Fed's 2% goal, and October brought strong hiring and faster pay. Fed officials keep saying more hikes are likely.
fed.watch: US inflation figures on Tuesday at 7:30 AM CT: hot prices would make a December hike close to certain, soft ones would revive doubts. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and has said more hikes may be needed. Two months of job losses have cut bets on a December hike to about one in three, which weighs on the loonie.
boc.priced: December: hold is the base case; hike about one in three.
boc.why: Dearer energy is lifting Canadian inflation, but the job market keeps weakening. That gives the bank reasons to move slowly.
boc.watch: The summary of the bank's October discussions on Tuesday at 12:30 PM CT, then oil prices, before the December 9 decision.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a 4–3 vote, though members agreed more tightening is likely. Rising unemployment has cut bets on a December hike to below even.
rbnz.priced: December: hike less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Price pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for patience.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on November 27 and what the next government means for the budget, before the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Because that hike is already expected, it gives the euro little fresh support.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the goal, mostly because of energy, but shoppers are cutting back and borrowing costs have already risen. That makes the bank wary of doing too much.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Thursday at 1:30 PM CT, and euro-area growth figures follow Friday, before the December 17 decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in October with one member wanting a hike, and markets expect it to raise rates in December. A hike would narrow the gap with other countries that keeps the yen weak.
boj.why: Inflation has been running above the 2% goal, and Governor Kazuo Ueda says real interest rates are still low, which leaves room to hike.
boj.watch: The summary of opinions from the October meeting tonight at 5:50 PM CT, a clue to how many members want a December move. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three members wanted to wait. Governor Michele Bullock hinted at a pause, so high rates are giving the Aussie less lift than usual.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high, but jobs are weakening and the board is split, so the bank wants to see how its hikes work first.
rba.watch: Australian jobs figures and the mood in global stock markets before the December 8 decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023. Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict ends, which supports the pound.
boe.priced: December: a second hike possible; no firm pricing yet.
boe.why: Energy and fuel costs have pushed UK inflation to its highest in about a year, and several officials want more hikes.
boe.watch: Bailey speaks today at 11:25 AM CT, and UK growth figures come Thursday at 1:00 AM CT, before the December 17 decision.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and says it can still sell francs if they get too strong. Higher October inflation has made another cut less likely, and markets mostly expect a hold in December.
snb.why: Inflation is low and a strong franc keeps import prices down, so the bank has no reason to hike. October's rise in inflation makes a cut less pressing.
snb.watch: How far the franc rises and the mood in stock markets before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by a Democratic Congress. Last Friday's strong jobs report revived bets that the Federal Reserve hikes in December.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike is the market's main expectation after hiring beat forecasts by a wide margin.
notes.inflation: US inflation is well above the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to keep raising rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. It trades close to its lowest level against the dollar since May 2025.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected, but euro rates still sit below US and UK rates, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Business surveys and shoppers in the euro area have weakened, with France's economy shrinking again.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money out of the region.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. Firm business surveys and sticky inflation back that case.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. Its safe-haven pull and a likely December rate hike give it some support.

notes.policy: At 1.25%, the Bank of Japan's rate is far below other major banks, even with a December hike likely.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did last week.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dear oil weighs on the yen.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, which could unwind fast if the mood turns.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, which supports it while the Iran war and the tech-stock slump linger.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks and firm commodity prices. Weak jobs and nervous stock markets still pushed it to its lowest since March last Friday.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause.
notes.growth: Australian business surveys have slipped and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells commodities abroad, and firm prices support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but two months of job losses have cut bets on more hikes.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, though markets now doubt a December move.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Rising costs for Canadian producers point to more inflation ahead.
notes.tot: Canada exports oil, so prices near $90 a barrel still support its earnings.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. Firm export prices help, and an election count that points to the same government staying gave it a small lift.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
